history.contentIn: The Stratospheric Controlled Perturbation Experiment (SCoPEx) was a Harvard University scientific proposal to study how tiny amounts of aerosol particles behave in the stratosphere. Principal investigator Frank Keutsch and collaborators including David Keith described the concept publicly, including at the American Geophysical Union Fall Meeting in 2017. The experiment was designed to improve computer models used to estimate risks and benefits of solar geoengineering (solar radiation management). It was not a test of deploying geoengineering and was not intended to cool the planet. The planned platform was a scientific balloon gondola with propellers, flying near 20 km altitude. A very small amount of material — on the order of 100 grams to less than 2 kilograms, typically calcium carbonate (a common mineral found in limestone and used in products such as toothpaste) — would be released into a small mixed volume roughly 1 km long and 100 meters in diameter. The gondola would then fly back through that plume to measure aerosol microphysics, chemistry, and light scattering. A 2021 platform test in Sweden, planned with the Swedish Space Corporation from Esrange, was a hardware test only: the SCoPEx Advisory Committee recommended suspending it pending societal engagement, and no particles were to be released. In March 2024 Harvard announced that Keutsch was no longer pursuing SCoPEx; the platform is expected to be repurposed for stratospheric research unrelated to solar geoengineering.

history.contentIn: Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) depend on sea ice as a platform for hunting seals. Arctic sea ice has declined in extent and thickness over the satellite era as the Arctic has warmed about twice as fast as the global mean (Arctic amplification). The IUCN and Arctic scientists treat loss of sea-ice hunting habitat as the primary long-term threat to the species. Some subpopulations have been relatively stable or better counted in recent surveys, which deniers sometimes quote as 'polar bears are fine.' That snapshot does not cancel the physical dependence on ice or projections of increased fasting and reduced cub survival as ice-free seasons lengthen, especially in southern parts of the range. Polar-bear numbers are not a single global census with low error; management units differ. Although certain subpopulations may show stable numbers in recent evaluations, this does not mitigate their dependence on sea ice or the forecasts of extended fasting periods and lower cub survival rates, especially in southern regions that experience longer ice-free seasons. It is crucial to recognize that polar bear populations differ across management units, as a singular global assessment fails to represent their true status. While issues such as conservation hunting quotas and pollution are prevalent, they do not overshadow the critical problem of diminishing sea ice. Assertions that polar bears are thriving due to chemtrails or that global warming is a myth, based on isolated population increases, lack scientific validity and overlook the essential ecological framework.
